title: Effect of Different Heat Treatment Procedures on the Corrosion Behavior of High-Manganese Austenitic Steels
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the effects of different heat treatment procedures on the corrosion behavior of high-manganese austenitic steel containing molybdenum. Five samples were prepared, including as-cast and heat-treated specimens, with varying processes such as tempering, single and double solution annealing, and aging. The study focuses on microstructural changes, carbide dissolution, and the formation of protective molybdenum-rich oxides. Microstructural analysis using scanning electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction was conducted to understand phase distribution. At the same time, corrosion resistance was evaluated through potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. The results reveal that double solution annealing leads to the most homogeneous microstructure and significantly enhances corrosion resistance by forming stable molybdenum oxide layers, underscoring the crucial role of molybdenum oxides in surface protection. Among the samples, the corrosion resistance ranked from best to worst is as follows: double solution-annealed (Ht-5), solution-annealed (Ht-3), aged after solution annealing (Ht-4), tempered (Ht-2), and as-cast (Ht-1). This highlights the crucial role of molybdenum oxides in surface protection. The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of advanced heat treatments in improving the corrosion resistance of high-manganese austenitic steels for industrial applications.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High-manganese austenitic steels are widely recognized for their exceptional combination of ductility and strength, which makes them indispensable in demanding industrial applications. These materials are particularly valued in mining, excavation, and agriculture sectors, where their high wear and impact resistance prove essential under aggressive working conditions. 1 , 2  The unique properties of these steels arise from their austenitic microstructure, stabilized by the addition of approximately 10–14% (wt%) manganese. However, during the casting process, the solidification conditions can lead to the formation of brittle carbide precipitates and other phases, limiting the usability of these steels in their as-cast form. 3  Consequently, heat treatment procedures often dissolve these carbides and homogenize the microstructure, enhancing mechanical properties.

On the other hand, heat treatments serve not only to dissolve secondary phases but also to improve the overall performance of high-manganese steels. 4  Mechanical properties such as tensile strength, impact resistance, and wear resistance can be significantly enhanced through controlled heat treatment processes. For example, Jafarian et al. 5  investigated the effect of austenitization temperature (between 1000 and 1225 °C) on Hadfield steel. Increasing the temperature enhanced yield strength, hardness, and wear resistance but reduced ductility and toughness due to grain growth. Azadi et al. 6  examined the effect of double solution heat treatment on the microstructure and mechanical properties of Hadfield steel, revealing that this treatment dissolved more carbides compared to standard solutions, resulting in finer grains and enhanced hardness when quenched at specific temperatures. Anijdan and Sabzi 7  studied the effect of different cooling media on the properties of austenitic Hadfield steel after heat treatment at 1100 °C. They reported that salt bath quenching reduced carbide content and led to improved toughness and fatigue life compared to pure water quenching.

Despite these advantages, high-manganese austenitic steels are often exposed to corrosive environments characterized by moisture and aggressive chemicals, which necessitate further research into improving their corrosion resistance. These steels suffer from poor corrosion resistance due to the fast dissolution of manganese, which has a lower reduction potential than iron, leading to a shorter lifespan. 8  For instance, Fajardo et al. 9  reported that increasing the manganese content from 21 to 28 wt% in TWIP austenitic manganese steels led to faster corrosion. This was due to the formation of Mn-based oxides, which are less protective than iron oxides, making the material more prone to corrosion in chloride-rich environments. In another study, Potgieter et al. 10  studied the corrosion behavior of different grades of WC-Co alloys and high-chromium white cast irons (HCWCI) compared with Hadfield steel in 1 M sulfuric acid. They reported that Hadfield steel exhibited the lowest corrosion resistance due to its high manganese content, which promotes hydrogen depolarization, causing the breakdown of the protective layer and resulting in localized corrosion, such as pitting and cracking around grain boundaries and carbide inclusion.

Given the harsh service conditions, especially in mining applications where both corrosion and wear damage pose a high risk, efforts have been directed toward optimizing the alloy’s corrosion resistance, sometimes at the expense of mechanical properties. Methods to increase the corrosion resistance in these steels include adding alloying elements, heat treatments, and surface coatings. 11 ,  12 ,  13 ,  14 – 15  For example, adding molybdenum plays a crucial role in enhancing both the corrosion resistance and toughness of manganese steels. 16  This improvement is achieved by stabilizing the matrix, delaying the precipitation of carbides, and contributing to the formation of protective oxide layers. Park et al. 8  explored the impact of chromium (Cr) addition on the corrosion behavior of Hadfield steel. They found that an optimized Cr content (2 wt%) facilitated the formation of a thin, adherent Cr-rich oxide layer, significantly improving corrosion resistance. However, a higher Cr content (3 wt%) led to the precipitation of coarse Cr-carbides (M 7 C 3 ), reducing corrosion resistance due to localized anodic dissolution near the carbides. Zellagui et al. 14  also aimed to improve the corrosion resistance of Hadfield steel by minimizing carbide formation during casting, with and without heat treatments. They found the as-cast sample had the lowest corrosion resistance, followed by the sample de-molded at 1000 °C and air-quenched, while the best performance was in the solution-annealed and water-quenched samples. These findings highlight the delicate balance between alloy composition and corrosion resistance.

Other studies have also highlighted the role of specific microstructural features in influencing corrosion behavior. Srivastava et al. 17  investigated the role of TiC particles in Hadfield steel, demonstrating that an increase in TiC content led to localized galvanic corrosion, thereby increasing the overall corrosion rate. Sabzi et al. 18  showed that higher melting temperatures resulted in lower carbide content and larger austenite grains, improving corrosion resistance by reducing micro-galvanic cells and high-energy grain boundaries. Additionally, they observed that welded joints with X-shaped geometries exhibited better corrosion resistance due to fewer carbides and larger grains compared to V-shaped joints, which suffered from increased grain boundaries and micro-galvanic corrosion. 19

While the literature presents various approaches to improving the corrosion resistance of high-manganese steels, the effects of heat treatments, particularly precipitation hardening, on the corrosion properties still need to be explored. Most existing studies focus on solution annealing treatments, leaving a knowledge gap in understanding the behavior of these steels under different heat treatment conditions, including tempering, single or double solution annealing, and aging. In this study, we aim to address this gap by investigating the effects of various heat treatment procedures on the corrosion and microstructural properties of high-molybdenum, high-manganese austenitic steels produced under industrial conditions. The research focuses on examining the relationship between heat treatment parameters and material performance through three primary objectives: (i) to analyze the microstructural changes with varying heat treatment conditions, (ii) to investigate the development and corrosion-resistant properties of molybdenum-rich oxide layers, and (iii) to evaluate and compare the corrosion resistance of specimens subjected to various thermal treatments.

sections.heading: Experimental Study
paragraphs: In this study, high-manganese austenitic steel was melted in a 3.5-ton industrial induction furnace and poured into a sand mold at approximately 1450 °C, as Balogun et al. 20  suggested. They reported that temperatures above 1450 °C cause alloy segregation and coarse carbides at grain boundaries, while lower temperatures (1380 °C) reduce fluidity and increase casting defects. The casting process utilized a green sand mold, as schematically illustrated in Figure  1 . The chemical composition of the cast part was analyzed using an optical emission spectroscopy (OES) device, with the results presented in Table  1 . Figure 1 Schematic illustration of casting and sample preparation processes. Table 1 Spectral Analysis Result of High-Manganese Austenitic Steel (%wt) Sample C Si Mn P S Ni Cr Mo Ti Cu Fe As-Cast 1.02 0.52 17.45 0.04 0.009 0.03 0.06 1.21 0.10 0.04 79.50

Samples with a dimension of 40 × 40 × 15 mm were cut from the cast part (60 × 60 × 300 mm), as depicted in Figure  1 , and then subjected to heat treatment according to the procedures outlined in Table  2 . This investigation analyzed five distinct samples: Ht-1 corresponds to the as-cast condition, where no heat treatment was applied. Ht-2 underwent tempering at 450 °C, while Ht-3 was solution-annealed and subsequently quenched in water. Ht-4 experienced a double solution annealing process, followed by quenching, and Ht-5 was subjected to solution annealing and then aged at 650 °C. Before solution annealing at 1100 °C, the samples were pre-heated to 650 °C and held for two hours to promote pearlite formation and refine the grain structure. Bandanadjaja et al. demonstrate that isothermal heating above 450 °C encourages pearlite formation at the grain boundaries, resulting in finer grains, which later transform into austenite during heating up to 1100 °C. 21 , 22  All heat treatments were performed using a Protherm electric resistance furnace with a controlled heating rate of 1.6 °C/min. Following the solution annealing process, the samples were rapidly quenched in water maintained at 25 °C to ensure proper cooling and prevent carbide precipitation. Table 2 Heat Treatment Procedure of Casting Sample Sample Tempering Solution annealing Aging Ht-1 – – – Ht-2 450 °C (2 h) – – Ht-3 1100 °C (2 h ) – Ht-4 1100 °C (2 h ) 650 °C (2 h ) Ht-5 1100 °C (2 h ) + 1100 (2 h) (2 h)°C –

The samples were sequentially sanded using 240, 320, 600, 1200, and 2500 mesh SiC sandpaper. After this, polishing was completed using 6, 1, and 0.05µ diamond paste. Surface roughness measurements performed with a Taylor-Hobson 2D profilometer revealed Ra values in the 0.04–0.05 µm range. Then, the samples were etched for 7 s using a 3% Nital solution for microstructural examination. Microstructural characterizations were conducted using a Jeol JSM 6060 scanning electron microscope (SEM) with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). Phase analysis was carried out using X-ray diffraction (XRD), and the identified phases were defined through X-pert High Score software. Brinell hardness measurements were performed using a Bulut Makina DIGIROCK RB model hardness tester, applying a 187.5 kgf load with a 2.5 mm carbide steel ball.

Before the corrosion test, samples were washed using ethanol, deionized water, and dried. Electrochemical tests were conducted using the classic three-electrode method with a Gamry 1010 E potentiostat electrochemical workstation. Before performing the potentiodynamic polarization tests, the samples were exposed to open circuit potential for 1800 seconds. A saturated calomel electrode (SCE) was used as the reference electrode, and a graphite electrode was the counter electrode. All corrosion tests were carried out in a 0.5 M NaCl solution. The scanning rate was set at 1 mV/s, with a potential range of −0.5 V to + 1.5 V. Corrosion potential (Ecor) and corrosion current (Icor) were calculated using Gamry Echem software. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests were conducted over 100 kHz to 10 MHz (Fig.  2 ). Figure 2 Schematic illustrations of the corrosion test setup.

sections.heading: Microstructural Characterization
paragraphs: The phase diagram in Figure  3 a, b shows the transformation of phases in high-manganese austenitic steel across different temperatures. The liquid phase exists above 1380 °C and transitions to solid phases at around 1255 °C. The FCC_A1 phase, representing the austenitic structure, forms upon solidification at 1255 °C and remains stable down to approximately 600 °C. The M 7 C 3  carbides start to form at approximately 868 °C, cementite (Fe 3 C) forms below 776 °C, and the BCC_A2 phase (ferrite) begins to form at around 568 °C. Additionally, MnS precipitates at around 1266 °C. The high-temperature phase observed between 1500 and 1600 °C could be related to complex titanium-rich compounds or intermetallic phases formed due to the high solubility of titanium at elevated temperatures. 3 , 23 Figure 3 Predicted of phase fraction calculated by Thermo-Calc Software for as-cast Fe-1C-0.5Si-17Mn-1.2Mo-0.1Ti steel.

Figure  4  shows the X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern of the as-cast high-Mn steel. Results exhibit characteristic peaks of the austenitic ( γ -Fe) phase, confirming its face-centered cubic (FCC) structure. The primary peaks are observed at approximately ~43.5° (2 θ ), ~50.6° (2 θ ), and ~74.6° (2 θ ), corresponding to the (111), (200), and (220) planes of the austenite phase, respectively. These peaks indicate the dominance of the austenitic structure in the as-cast condition. A minor peak at approximately 44.5–45° (2 θ ) has been identified, attributed to the presence of (Fe,Mn) 3 C carbides. The formation of these carbides is typical in Hadfield steel due to its high carbon and manganese content. This XRD analysis confirms that the as-cast Hadfield steel primarily consists of an austenitic phase with minor quantities of (Fe,Mn) 3 C carbides, indicative of secondary phases formed during casting and cooling processes. This finding aligns with existing literature on the crystallographic characteristics of austenite and cementite phases in high-manganese steels. 23 Figure 4 XRD analysis of the as-cast sample (Ht-1).

As shown in Figure  5 , the optical (a-b) and SEM images (c-d) and MAP analysis of the as-cast high-manganese austenitic steel sample reveal significant microstructural characteristics. The slow cooling effect within the mold post-casting forms large colonies with a pearlitic appearance, identified as cementite (Fe 3 C) dispersed within the austenitic matrix and along the grain boundaries (Figure  5 a-d). Both molybdenum (Mo) and titanium (Ti) are strong carbide-forming elements that easily integrate into the molten alloy. Molybdenum, in particular, forms M 7 C 3  carbides (Mo-rich carbides) that stabilize and precipitate throughout the matrix. These Mo-rich carbides (white regions) are essential for enhancing the mechanical properties of the material by reinforcing the matrix and significantly improving wear resistance. Moreover, the MAP analysis highlights the titanium (Ti)-based phases distributed in the microstructure. This phase indicated the formation of randomly dispersed TiN or/and TiCN particulates due to their high affinity for carbon. Also, this phase might be the first solidified phase in the alloy because of the high melting point. 24  Due to their high stability and hardness, these titanium-based particulates significantly contribute to the overall strengthening of the alloy by grain refinement. 25 Figure 5 (a-b) Optical micrographs, (c-d) SEM images, EDS and MAP analysis of Ht-1 (as-cast) sample.

Figure  6  presents SEM images of the samples after the heat treatment of the Ht-1 (as-cast) specimen. No significant microstructural changes were observed in the Ht-2 sample after heat treatment at 450 °C, as this temperature was insufficient to dissolve pearlite and re-precipitate any other phases within the microstructure. The carbides were dissolved after the solution treatment at 1100 °C, whereas TiC particles remained in the microstructure (Ht-3). The microstructures of the Ht-4 and Ht-5 samples were comparable to that of the Ht-3 sample. In both samples, Ht-3 and Ht-5, the carbides present in the as-cast condition were fully dissolved, with only TiC particles persisting within the microstructure. Notably, during the aging process at 650 °C, no bulk or large carbides were observed, unlike the needle-like or pearlite-like carbides commonly reported in the literature at even lower temperatures. Instead, a few amounts of very fine, globular carbides were present, dispersed within the austenitic matrix. This fine distribution of carbides can be attributed to the high molybdenum content in the alloy, which likely inhibits and limits the growth of secondary carbides by stabilizing the austenitic matrix, ensuring a more homogeneous microstructure. Figure 6 SEM images of samples in different heat treatment conditions.

As some examples from the literature research, Cui et al. 26  investigated the effect of aging temperature on solution-annealed and water-quenched standard Hadfield steel (ASTM A128 Gr. B2), which lacks alloying elements such as molybdenum and chromium. They reported that no significant microstructural changes were observed at 400 °C. However, as the temperature increased to 500 °C, fine needle-shaped carbides began to form along the grain boundaries. By 600 °C, the carbide precipitation became more pronounced, leading to a more uniform distribution of needle- and rod-shaped carbides throughout the microstructure. Feng et al. 27  studied the effect of aging temperature on Fe-16Mn-1.3C-0.3V high-manganese steel (with similar manganese content to our study but higher carbon and no Mo alloying). They reported that fine globular carbides began to precipitate at 350 °C, a lower temperature compared to other studies explained before. Similarly, they also indicated that needle-like carbides appeared along grain boundaries at 500 °C, becoming more pronounced and coarser by 550 °C, while the globular carbides diminished with increasing temperatures. In another study, Sun et al. 28  investigated the effects of aging temperature following solution annealing and water quenching on the microstructure of alloyed high-manganese steel (Cr 1.62%, Mo 0.61%, and V 0.24%). They revealed that carbide precipitation occurred between 550 and 600 °C. In addition to carbide precipitation, pearlite formed at 650 °C, with the maximum amount of carbide and pearlite observed at this temperature. Compared to these studies, the significant effect of high molybdenum content in limiting carbide re-precipitation is apparent in our research. This makes Mo-alloyed high-manganese steels highly suitable for applications requiring weld repairs or those that demand excellent toughness and high tensile strength.

sections.heading: Hardness Test
paragraphs: The hardness values of the samples are illustrated in Figure  7 . The as-cast sample (Ht-1) exhibited a hardness of 194.9 HB. Following heat treatment at 450 °C, the hardness increased by approximately 11%. In contrast, a slight decrease in hardness was observed in the samples that underwent solution treatment. This reduction can likely be attributed to the dissolution of carbides present in the as-cast sample, which leads to a more homogeneous austenitic microstructure. Nonetheless, traces of fine molybdenum carbides may remain at the grain boundaries after solution treatment, but they are not expected to impact tensile or notch strength significantly. Figure 7 Hardness test results of as-cast high-manganese austenitic steel and its various heat-treated conditions.

Following either the casting process or solution treatment, a 10-15% increase in hardness was observed due to the aging process at 650 °C. This increase can be attributed to the fine dispersion of (Fe,Mn) 3 C carbides throughout the microstructure, which aligns with the literature indicating that similar treatments promote the formation of finely dispersed (Fe) 3 C carbides, enhancing hardness. 29   The double solution annealing at 1100 °C (Ht-5) also resulted in a more homogeneous austenitic structure, with no trace of fine carbides, compared to the single solution annealing process. While the single quenching operation (Ht-3) produced a primarily austenitic microstructure, fine carbides may remain partially undissolved, particularly along grain boundaries. In contrast, the double quenching process not only facilitated greater homogeneity in carbide distribution but also resulted in a more uniform hardness profile (Ht-5).

sections.heading: Corrosion Behavior
paragraphs: Figure  8 a displays the OCP (open circuit potential) measurements of the samples over 1800 seconds. These OCP measurements, conducted in a specific corrosive environment, provide valuable insights into the thermodynamic stability of the sample surfaces. In this context, OCP values can be interpreted as corrosion potentials, indicating the surface's ability to resist corrosion. 30 , 31  The graphs show that all samples initially shift toward the anodic region before stabilizing. Among them, Ht-1 and Ht-2 exhibit more positive OCP values, suggesting forming a more stable and protective surface film. 32  Both samples reach a steady-state condition after a longer period, particularly in the 0.5 M NaCl solution, indicating that their passive layers are thicker and more resistant to the corrosive environment. This increased stability may be attributed to carbides within the grain interiors and boundaries, which initially offer some protective effect. However, the heterogeneous microstructure eventually leads to lower long-term corrosion resistance. Figure 8 (a) OCP graph and (b) Tafel curves of the as-cast high-manganese austenitic steel and its various heat-treated conditions.

In contrast, Ht-3, Ht-4, and Ht-5 show more pronounced initial shifts toward the active region, with OCP stabilization occurring more rapidly. This is particularly evident in Ht-3 and Ht-5, which underwent solution annealing. The heat treatment resulted in more homogeneous austenitic structures with fewer carbides, allowing for quicker but more stable passive film formation on the surface. In the case of Ht-5, which underwent double solution annealing, the nearly fully austenitic structure significantly improved corrosion resistance, as indicated by faster OCP stabilization and lower current densities observed in subsequent electrochemical tests. The faster stabilization observed in Ht-3 and Ht-5, along with the intermediate behavior of Ht-4 due to the aging process at 650 °C following solution annealing, can be attributed to their more uniform microstructures and reduced carbide content, which facilitated the more efficient formation of protective passive layers.

Figure  8 b shows the Tafel curves obtained from the potentiodynamic polarization tests. The Tafel curves (together with Table  3 ) reveal that Ht-1 and Ht-2 exhibit more positive corrosion potentials, indicating higher corrosion resistance despite carbides in their microstructures. However, when comparing the current densities, Ht-3, Ht-4, and Ht-5 demonstrate lower current densities, which directly correspond to lower corrosion rates, indicating better corrosion resistance due to their more homogeneous microstructures. 2  Since current density is a critical parameter in the kinetics of corrosion and serves as a direct measure of the corrosion rate, 33  these lower current densities clearly reflect the improved corrosion performance of the samples. Table 3 Corrosion Parameters Obtained from Tafel Curves Sample E cor  mV I cor  µA/cm 2 Cr (mpy) Ht-1 − 726.508 6.152 3.136 Ht-2 − 726.019 6.029 3.074 Ht-3 − 854.637 3.597 1.834 Ht-4 − 836.179 3.839 1.957 Ht-5 − 787.81 3.143 1.602

The Ht-5, which underwent double solution annealing, exhibits the lowest current densities, reflecting the formation of a fully austenitic structure and the most uniform passive layer, thereby providing the best corrosion protection. Although Ht-4, which was aged after solution annealing, also demonstrates relatively low current densities, they are slightly higher than those of Ht-3 and Ht-5, likely due to minor carbide precipitation during the aging process. These trends align with the findings reported in the literature, such as the work by Zellagui et al. 14 , which highlights that solution annealing enhances corrosion resistance by reducing carbide content, whereas extended aging can slightly diminish corrosion resistance due to carbide precipitation. Thus, the lower the current density, the slower the corrosion rate, making it a vital indicator of the corrosion behavior in these samples. 34

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was utilized to gain deeper insights into the corrosion kinetics. As shown in Figure  9 , the Nyquist plots reveal semicircular impedance curves for all samples, signifying a charge-transfer controlled mechanism. It is widely recognized that in Nyquist plots, the size of the capacitive loop is directly related to the corrosion resistance of the material, with a larger loop indicating better resistance. 35  Among the tested samples, Ht-5, which underwent double solution annealing, exhibits the most giant capacitive loop, pointing to its superior corrosion resistance. The corrosion resistance follows a decreasing trend in the order of Ht-4, Ht-3, Ht-2, and Ht-1. These findings confirm that a combination of solution annealing and subsequent aging treatments markedly enhances the corrosion resistance of high-manganese austenitic steel. Figure 9 Nyquist plots show the corrosion behavior of as-cast high-manganese austenitic steel and its various heat-treated conditions.

The experimental parameters obtained by fitting the curves to the CPE model are summarized in Table  4 . Given the non-ideal capacitive behavior observed at the metal/solution interface, as demonstrated by the Nyquist curves, the constant phase element (CPE) was employed in place of an ideal capacitor. 36  In this model, Rs signifies the solution resistance, Rct represents the charge-transfer resistance, and CPE represents the constant phase element. Both Rs and Rct are related to the diameter of the Nyquist curves, with higher Rct values indicating increased corrosion resistance. 37  The similarity in the capacitive curves suggests that corrosion progresses similarly across all samples, as supported by the OCP and Tafel curves. This consistent corrosion behavior may be linked to the dissolution of carbides and other phases following heat treatments. The elevated Rct value observed in the Ht-4 sample likely results from the formation of precipitates in the microstructure during aging. These precipitates, forming thinner and more uniformly than the secondary phases present in the as-cast condition, contribute to the higher Rct value by increasing internal resistance. Figure  10  presents an SEM image and elemental mapping of the corroded surface of the Ht-1 sample (as-cast high-manganese steel). The microstructural analysis reveals the presence of eutectic-like phases, carbides, and other secondary phases embedded within the matrix. These phases create a heterogeneous microstructure with regions of differing electrochemical potentials, forming localized galvanic cells. Previous studies show that differences in phase and elemental distribution in manganese steel cause a significant change in potential value during different stages of corrosion. 38 , 39  Consequently, galvanic corrosion is concentrated around these phases, contributing to the overall corrosion mechanism. Due to multiple phases, the dissolution process in this intricate structure occurs at a slower pace, as reflected in the OCP curves, where the Ht-1 sample exhibits more positive corrosion potentials. This suggests the gradual formation of a protective film on the surface, although it develops more slowly compared to heat-treated samples. Figure 10 Corroded surfaces of as-cast high-manganese austenitic steel (Ht-1 sample).

The elemental mapping further corroborates these findings, with manganese, iron, molybdenum, and oxygen indicating the spatial distribution of phases within the corroded area. The oxygen distribution highlights the regions where oxidation occurs, which correlates with the corrosion sites. Additionally, the detection of Na and Cl, originating from the electrolyte solution, suggests localized corrosion in the form of pitting, particularly in regions vulnerable to attack due to the aggressive environment. The slow development of the passive layer, as shown in the elemental map, aligns with the OCP results, where the passive film forms but offers less protection due to the galvanic activity within the heterogeneous microstructure. This complex corrosion mechanism likely accounts for the relatively higher corrosion rates observed in the as-cast sample during electrochemical testing.

Figure  11  illustrates an SEM image of the corroded surface of the Ht-5 sample, which was subjected to double solution annealing. As discussed in the microstructure section, this heat treatment process dissolves carbides, resulting in a more uniform microstructure that greatly enhances corrosion resistance. However, titanium carbides (TiC), which form during solidification, remain undissolved after treatment but have minimal corrosion effects. The key factor in corrosion protection is molybdenum, which contributes by forming stable, protective oxides. Yan et al. emphasized that molybdenum oxides contribute to forming a stable passive film, effectively mitigating the detrimental effects of chloride ions on corrosion resistance. 39  Similar observations have been reported in various studies. For instance, Grajcar et al. 40  noted that single-phase high-manganese steel exhibited slightly less dissolution in H 2 SO 4  compared to high-manganese steel containing secondary phases, although the difference was not particularly significant. This behavior is likely influenced by the elemental composition, microstructural phases, and their morphology, distribution, and fraction. 41 , 42  Research indicates that elements such as Ni and Cu tend to accumulate in corrosion products during the initial stages of corrosion, while Cr and Mo become concentrated at the interface between the matrix and the corrosion products during later stages. 38  The synergistic interactions between elements within the microstructure are also known to affect corrosion behavior significantly. 43 , 44  For example, chromium is widely used to enhance corrosion resistance in steels due to its strong affinity for oxygen and its ability to form a passive oxide layer on the surface. 45  Also, chromium acts as a barrier to cation penetration generated by manganese-rich compounds, stabilizing the corrosion rate. 46  Molybdenum exhibits a similar effect; its stable oxides reduce cation permeability and slow corrosion. 47  Furthermore, molybdenum enhances the passivation ability of the oxide film in chloride-rich environments. 48 , 49  SEM analysis in this study confirms that molybdenum significantly influences corrosion resistance. The molybdenum-rich oxide layer observed in the SEM images forms a uniform coating that effectively acts as a barrier against further corrosion. Heat treatment facilitates the homogeneous distribution of molybdenum within the microstructure, enhancing the stability of the oxide layer and improving its passivation properties. These findings emphasize the critical role of molybdenum in stabilizing the passive layer and mitigating chloride-induced corrosion. Figure 11 Corroded surfaces of double solution-annealed high-manganese austenitic steel (Ht-5 sample).

In particular, the double solution-annealed Ht-5 sample demonstrates the superior protective effects of molybdenum. The uniform distribution of molybdenum-rich oxides in this sample underscores its suitability for use in harsh environments. Electrochemical analyses further support these observations, with the Ht-5 sample consistently exhibiting the lowest corrosion rates and the most robust protective characteristics, as evidenced by its impedance and polarization data. These results align with existing literature, highlighting molybdenum's role in enhancing oxide stability, reducing cation permeability, and preventing localized pitting. 50 , 51  The significance of this mechanism extends beyond the current study, offering a framework for optimizing high-manganese steel compositions and treatments for corrosion-resistant applications in mining and marine industries.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study aimed to evaluate the impact of various heat treatment processes on the corrosion resistance of high-manganese austenitic steels. The findings of this investigation can be summarized as follows: Solution annealing significantly improved the uniformity of the microstructure and reduced the presence of harmful carbides compared to the as-cast condition. Molybdenum-rich oxide layers played a critical role in enhancing corrosion resistance by creating a stable, protective surface layer. Double solution annealing (Ht-5) produced the most corrosion-resistant sample due to the formation of a homogeneous microstructure and stable molybdenum oxide layers.

This study provides new insights into the role of molybdenum and heat treatment processes in optimizing the corrosion resistance of high-manganese steels. The findings have practical implications for industries where both wear resistance and corrosion resistance are critical, such as mining and heavy machinery production. The demonstrated improvements in corrosion performance through advanced heat treatments may guide future developments in the manufacturing and treatment of high-manganese steels.
